wi_3_godfather_boulder.blurb: The biggest block in the Box Canyon group at Governor Dodge State Park, near Dodgeville, and widely considered the park's best boulder. It is tall, steep and overhanging, with a dozen problems running from an easy V0 corner up to a V7, and the bulk of them landing between V4 and V6. That makes it a better stop for climbers with some strength than for first-timers, though a couple of lower grades give warm-up options. Bring plenty of pads and a spotter, because the top-out and landings are serious. Expect a short walk on a footpath off the road.

wi_farewell_to_arms_wall.blurb: A tucked-away wall at Devil's Lake in Wisconsin's Baraboo Range, sitting directly beneath the Red Nose formation on the East Bluff. A dozen routes, almost all of them traditional with a single top-rope line, span roughly 5.4 to 5.11, with a handful of easy and moderate lines and a cluster of harder ones in the 5.10 and 5.11 range. Climbs are short, around 35 feet on the main face, with tree anchors at the top. It tends to be quieter than the headline walls nearby, so it suits a party wanting a bit of solitude and a gear-protected outing.

wi_12_anthrax_wall.blurb: A tall grey face on the main spine's north end at Petenwell Rock, the sandstone crag outside Necedah in central Wisconsin. Twelve routes mix trad, sport and top-rope, from 5.7 into the low 5.11s; the easier half is mostly gear-protected and only a few lines are bolted, so sport climbers will find a short list. Because the wall stays shaded it can be a decent pick on hot days, though it sits close to the road and can be noisy. The base is a very short walk from the north end of the ridge, so it fits a quick session.

wi_mike_s_boulder.blurb: A large block on the Wisconsin side of Interstate Park, right along the St. Croix River, split by a sloping ridge that runs up the middle of the face. A dozen problems cover a wide spread: a few easy ones to the left for warming up, a middle group around V2 to V6, and several hard testpieces up to V10. The park's rock is basalt, with plenty of texture in places. A short trail and a hop across rocks at the river brings you to the base, and the setting is scenic, with easy access to other problems nearby.

wi_4_the_pantry.blurb: A scatter of small rocks on the south side of Misery Gully, just below Misery Rocks on Devil's Lake's West Bluff. The twelve routes are traditional with a few top-ropes, running from beginner-level scrambles around 5.1 to 5.4 through the middle grades and up to a couple of lines at 5.10. The setting is wooded and shaded in summer, and it is a handy fallback when the neighbouring Misery Rocks is busy with guided groups. Reaching it takes a hike up the West Bluff Trail and a descent down a slot, so allow time and be careful on the steep ground.

wi_main_park_west_ridge.blurb: The taller of the two ridges in Westby's small town park in west-central Wisconsin, where sandstone boulders rich in slopers sit a short stroll from the car, beyond the playground. Twelve problems run from V1 up to V9, clustered at easier and middle grades with a few hard ones at the top end, and some of the highest lines in the park live here. Fall is the best season; spring and summer can be damp, and the rock dries slowly after rain. Moss and lichen come back fast if the problems go unclimbed.

wi_main_area.blurb: The main bouldering zone at Ledge Park in Horicon, on the Niagara Escarpment, a maze of ledges and pillars that stretches north from the parking lot. Twelve problems span V0 to V7, but most sit in the V2 range, so it works well for beginners and for climbers wanting volume rather than a project. Quality is average, with a few standouts, and ledges partway up tend to keep the harder lines scarce. It is a pleasant stop with families nearby on busy days; weekdays are quieter.

wi_main_park_east_ridge.blurb: A lower ridgeline along the east side of the small town park in Westby, Wisconsin, easy to spot from the parking lot and shorter than its western neighbour. Its twelve sandstone boulder problems are friendly: from the easiest vertical-and-below grades through V3, with most around V2. That makes it a good place for beginners, kids and warm-ups. The rock is slopey, and moss and lichen build up quickly if it sits unused. Fall is the best time to visit, and the stone dries slowly after rain.

_conflicts.wi_main_area: Stored rock is dolomite but the Ledge Park page (https://mountainproject.com/area/106176300/ledge-park) says limestone; no rock named.
